doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Teaching at the Lenox School of Jazz and meeting David Baker
summary: Schuller and Lewis brought him to Lenox, where he met Baker; Brookmeyer's recent European school failed.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: It was around this same time also that you were teaching at the Lenox School of Jazz.

This, too, was an outgrowth of the alliance with Gunther Schuller and John Lewis who were a part of a faction that brought about this thing at Lenox. They brought me into the fold on the level of teaching, and that’s how that all came about and how I first met your wonderful husband, David Baker. I had heard about David, but I think that was the first time we had encountered each other on a one-on-one basis.

That was one hell of a school. I was telling Lida and them that it was the prototype of what a school could be. There has since never been anything like that because they were never able to assemble the kind of people that they had at that particular school – to have you and Max, the Modern Jazz Quartet, and Gunther and all of
these people who had all these huge reputations. The only way it could have happened would have been in the summer.
Are you aware, David and Lida, of the attempt that Bob Brookmeyer made just recently to have such an environment?
Yeah, sponsored by the Rotterdam government or something like that. It looked very good for him for a while. Then it fell through the cracks, for reasons I never understood.
I was with him in January.
Oh, really? Did he run by you what happened? Its downfall?

No, he was pretty dejected. This was in January at IAJE [at the annual conference of the International Association for Jazz Education]. I talked to him at length. I think the expense involved and the fact that Bobby was also trying to do it by bringing a lot of American musicians at pretty good prices because of carrying [them] over there [might have been part of it]. But I thought that what you guys did there [at the Lenox School of Jazz] was something that revolutionized a lot of young people because it was like Who’s Who [in] the student body at those things, too.
